One week after Democrats pulled off a historic blue wave in the midterm elections, a bunch of them a) got stuck in traffic; b) had other appointments; c) didn’t realize how to count and botched an opportunity to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

   Eleven Democrats missed a roll-call vote Tuesday , which allowed the impeachment proceedings against Hegseth to essentially vanish. If those 11 had shown up and all voted to proceed with impeachment, it’s possible Hegseth would be the third cabinet member in U.S. history to face such a fate.

   Some Democrats were livid. Other Democrats were quick to offer excuses about why they weren’t so quick to vote.

   (On Wednesday, a group Hegseth was in was reprimanded by a guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery and told to show respect.)

   Welcome to the lame-duck Congress of 2026, where there will likely be a lot of woulda, coulda, shoulda, and not a lot of actual legislating.

   Democrats for the most part had a jovial week. A lot of the newly elected members (who won’t be sworn in until January) came to town for orientation and selfies and lunches and glad-handing. What the lawmakers who are still in Congress didn’t do a lot of this week though was, well, vote on time.

   Is this just a little innocent hiccup or a sign of what’s to come in the “laissez faire” leadership of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.)?

   It might be easy to say, “This never would have happened under Nancy Pelosi,” except for the fact that Pelosi, who is retiring after this term, is one of the 11 members who missed the Tuesday night vote.

Damian Paletta
 
Disorganized Democrats Learn a Hard Lesson in Washington Gridlock
 
Plus, JD Vance weighs meeting with Iran’s hard-line security chief, and RFK Jr.’s undeclared luxury-yacht trip around Greece
 
 
ALEX WONG/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. One week after Democrats pulled off a historic blue wave in the midterm elections, a bunch of them a) got stuck in traffic; b) had other appointments; c) didn’t realize how to count and botched an opportunity to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

 

Eleven Democrats missed a roll-call vote Tuesday, which allowed the impeachment proceedings against Hegseth to essentially vanish. If those 11 had shown up and all voted to proceed with impeachment, it’s possible Hegseth would be the third cabinet member in U.S. history to face such a fate.

 

Some Democrats were livid. Other Democrats were quick to offer excuses about why they weren’t so quick to vote.

 

(On Wednesday, a group Hegseth was in was reprimanded by a guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery and told to show respect.)

 

Welcome to the lame-duck Congress of 2026, where there will likely be a lot of woulda, coulda, shoulda, and not a lot of actual legislating.

 

Democrats for the most part had a jovial week. A lot of the newly elected members (who won’t be sworn in until January) came to town for orientation and selfies and lunches and glad-handing. What the lawmakers who are still in Congress didn’t do a lot of this week though was, well, vote on time.

 

Is this just a little innocent hiccup or a sign of what’s to come in the “laissez faire” leadership of Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D., N.Y.)?

 

It might be easy to say, “This never would have happened under Nancy Pelosi,” except for the fact that Pelosi, who is retiring after this term, is one of the 11 members who missed the Tuesday night vote.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Jensen Huang: U.S. officials have repeatedly raised concerns about his influence with President Trump and the Nvidia CEO’s posture toward China.

 

Scott Colom: The Democrat will become the first Black senator from the state since the Reconstruction era following the Civil War.

 

Trump’s Thursday: The president will hold policy meetings and tape a couple of interviews.

What I’m Following

 
 
TOM BRENNER/PRESS POOL
 

JD Vance considers direct talks with Iran’s security chief. The vice president is positioning himself as Washington’s lead negotiator over the Iran war. In October, he wrote to Mohsen Rezaei, the hard-line secretary of Iran’s top security body, asking for a meeting. No date has been set, but a direct meeting between the vice president and top Iranian security officials would show the lengths Vance is willing to go to try to end the war.

 

The donor who funded RFK Jr.’s flights also hosted him on his yacht. The health secretary sailed around Greece aboard a luxury yacht owned by his friend Gavin de Becker, part of a 2025 vacation that included $45,000 in airfare. The yacht trips weren’t disclosed in ethics filings. Senate Democrats say they are opening a probe into de Becker’s gifts to Kennedy which we reported earlier this year.

 

Democrats aim to sink Trump’s battleship plans. Fresh from wins in the midterm elections, lawmakers are taking aim at the president’s pet defense projects. Democrats are planning to pare back some of the Trump administration’s defense priorities, including the “Trump-class” warships, the renaming of the Defense Department, and the “Golden Dome,” a missile-and-drone shield around the country.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• “The ass-kicking we needed”: Some Republicans welcomed the party’s midterms drubbing as an opportunity for a reset.

 

• Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved to a military base after receiving threats from Iran.

 

• The White House warned Democrats over investigations in the next Congress.
